items.item: An impact analysis reads the lineage graph outward from a chosen asset; downstream answers what breaks, upstream answers where a wrong value came from.
Table-level lineage says which datasets are connected; column-level lineage says which of them actually read the specific field being changed.

items.item: Assessing the incident's impact is the first step of an active-incident response, with mitigation prioritized above root cause.

at.step: Reveal: a failed partition spreads differently

items.item: This topic's table-level and column-level walks are a BFS/DFS graph traversal exactly as Chapter 1's own refresher topic named it, applied here to a lineage graph instead of a task DAG — the same algorithm, a different kind of node.

The deduplicated, per-owner notification this topic builds is the same deduplication-and-routing idea topic 3 introduced for paging, now applied to a lineage-derived affected-table list instead of a firing alert.

The column this topic tracks through a rename is exactly the kind of tag-propagation path topic 4 first named for sensitivity tags — here the thing propagating is the column's own identity through a lineage graph, not a classification tag, but the propagate-along-the-graph mechanism is the same shape.

The catalog this topic's notifications resolve each affected table's owner from is topic 10's own catalog, and the technical-vs-business split that topic drew (what a crawler can see vs what a person must name) is echoed here in the gap between the graph's table-level reach and what a human still has to judge in a deprecation sign-off.

The deprecation workflow's sign-off gate is the same automate-vs-human split topic 13 drew: whether a table has live dependents is a rule a program checks for itself, but whose sign-off actually counts and when a table is safe to retire still runs through the governance model topic 13 built.

DataHub's own distinction between table-level and column-level lineage precision is exactly what this topic's two walk functions demonstrate with a real, planted graph rather than describing in the abstract: the three named false positives are the concrete cost of table-level imprecision DataHub's blog only states in general terms.

at.step: Reveal: walking the graph, column by column

items.item: The Google SRE Workbook's own priority order (assess impact, then mitigate, with root cause last) is why this topic treats stale propagation as a table-level, not column-level, question: a failed partition needs its blast marked wide and fast, not narrowed precisely first.

at.step: Reveal: a failed partition spreads differently

items.item: The uninstrumented partner reader is this topic's own worked instance of topic 11's own disclosed limit (lineage-coverage-gaps): a genuine consumer with no OpenLineage event behind it is invisible to every algorithm in this topic, not a hypothetical edge case.

Marquez's own node model (dataset, dataset field, or job, each with in/out edges) is the same three-kind-of-node shape this topic's own EDGES structure encodes directly in Python, without calling Marquez itself, since this sandbox has no connected Marquez server.

at.step: Reveal: walking the graph, table by table

items.item: The ten real asserted numbers in this topic's own lab run (three catalog entries, fourteen table-level, eleven column-level, three named false positives, ten stale, four notifications, two deprecation outcomes) are each a direct output of a graph-traversal function, not a hand-typed illustration — the same discipline every topic in this chapter has held to.
